name: Return on assets (ROA)
title: Return on assets (ROA): Formula and Worked Example
description: Return on assets compares net income for a reporting period with average total book assets supporting that income.
definition: Return on assets compares net income for a reporting period with average total book assets supporting that income.
explanation: Period ROA divides net income by average total assets. A company with $120,000 income and $1,000,000 average book assets has 12% ROA for that reporting period; this worksheet does not automatically annualize it.
formula: ROA = net income / average total assets. Two-point average = (beginning + ending assets) / 2. With positive denominators, ROA = net profit margin × asset turnover.
formulaNote: Same-period unadjusted net income / average book total assets in USD. A two-point average or supplied documented average; signed income and target rates, explicit zero-denominator states. No automatic annualization, EBIT/interest adjustments, market asset values, industry benchmarks, forecast or investment rating.

pitfall.title: Keep the comparison basis consistent
pitfall.text: A shrinking or poorly sampled asset denominator can increase ROA without improving operating results. A quarterly ROA is not automatically an annual ROA, and zero assets do not imply a real 0% return.

name: Mortgage assumption
title: Mortgage assumption: Formula and Worked Example
description: A mortgage assumption transfers an existing loan obligation to a purchaser under terms permitted by the lender and applicable program. Its remaining balance can be less than the home purchase price.
definition: A mortgage assumption transfers an existing loan obligation to a purchaser under terms permitted by the lender and applicable program. Its remaining balance can be less than the home purchase price.
explanation: An assumption comparison needs the purchase-price gap, remaining old-loan term and any second loan. Compare both options at the same holding horizon, including fees, interest and debt still owed; a lower initial payment alone does not prove a lower financing cost.
formula: Gap loan = purchase price − assumed balance − buyer cash. Same-horizon financing cost = paid fees + interest. Cash at closing + P&I paid + remaining debt = purchase price + financing cost.
formulaNote: One hypothetical USD purchase with an assumed fixed-rate amortizing loan and optional fixed-rate gap financing; compare with one new loan at the same cash contribution and monthly horizon. Fees paid separately. No underwater transaction, escrow/insurance, FHA/VA fee table, eligibility, APR, entitlement/release decision, appreciation or cash opportunity return.

example.title: Compare the same 150,000 cash contribution
example.intro: price: 450000; assumed_balance: 300000; assumed_rate: 3; remaining_months: 240; assumption_fees: 3000; new_rate: 6.5; new_months: 360; new_fees: 6000; horizon_months: 60
steps: 450,000 price − 300,000 assumed balance = 150,000 cash toward price.
Add 3,000 assumption fees for 153,000 cash at closing. The alternative uses the same down payment, plus its own fees.
example.answer: Purchase price minus assumed balance: 150,000.00 under these assumptions.
example.assumptions: One hypothetical USD purchase with an assumed fixed-rate amortizing loan and optional fixed-rate gap financing; compare with one new loan at the same cash contribution and monthly horizon. Fees paid separately. No underwater transaction, escrow/insurance, FHA/VA fee table, eligibility, APR, entitlement/release decision, appreciation or cash opportunity return.

pitfall.title: Keep the comparison basis consistent
pitfall.text: An old low-rate loan can require a large cash gap or an expensive second loan. Do not reset its remaining term or treat unpaid principal at the horizon as savings. Approval, release of liability and any VA entitlement substitution are separate questions.
